issues.description: Unclear contributor status in CRediT front matter: The CRediT table introduces So Chi Liu as a contributor even though the preceding title page, authorship declaration, and 'Full details of all authors' table identify only Yik Chun Wong and Gilad Feldman. Because the table assigns verification-related roles, the document should make the author/non-author status of this contributor clear for attribution and accountability.

issues.subcategory: Abstract treats simulated data as findings
issues.description: Abstract treats simulated data as findings: The Abstract treats the randomized Qualtrics dummy output as if it were empirical evidence about the target phenomenon. Although the bracketed note flags the results as simulated, statements such as “found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect” make substantive inferential claims that placeholder random data cannot support.
issues.quote:
[IMPORTANT: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

The identifiable victim effect is a phenomenon characterized by the human's tendency to give out more aid to a specific victim than to a group of statistical individuals. In this pre-registered study, we conducted a replication of Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic's (2007) Studies 1 and 3 to examine the effect of deliberative thinking on debiasing the identifiable victim effect. We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey ( $\mathrm{N}=1000$ ) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: Abstract misstates the extension hypothesis
issues.description: Abstract misstates the extension hypothesis: The Abstract appears to reverse the extension hypothesis. Hypothesis 6 later predicts that identifiable victims elicit higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims, but the Abstract says the results supported a hypothesis of lower perceived impact for identifiable or joint identifiable/statistical presentations. The simulated post-hoc result reported later also only shows statistical victims rated higher than the joint condition, so it does not support the stated Hypothesis 6.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: Opening definition sets up the wrong comparison
issues.description: Opening definition sets up the wrong comparison: The phrase “an identifiable and unidentifiable individual” sets up a comparison between two single victims. The manuscript’s design compares identifiable-victim, statistical-victim, and joint information conditions. Align this section with that target contrast: greater giving to a single identifiable victim than to anonymous statistical victims, with identified groups treated as a related boundary case rather than the main comparison.
issues.quote: The phenomenon of disproportional generosity provoked from an identifiable and unidentifiable individual is supported by numerous empirical research (Friedrich \& McGuire, 2010; Lee \& Feeley, 2016; Solvic, 2010). Kogut and Ritov (2005a) claimed that this effect is particularly restricted to a single target with his or her name, age, or face displayed as more generosity would be elicited compared with a group of identified victims.

issues.subcategory: The proportion-dominance explanation assumes complete rescue
issues.description: The proportion-dominance explanation assumes complete rescue: This mechanism is stated more strongly than the donation task allows. A donation to one named victim does not establish that the donor saves 1 out of 1 lives. If a $5 donation covers only a fraction q of the needed aid, or only raises the chance of help, the relevant proportion is q/1 rather than 100%. The same issue appears in the statistical-victim sentence: the number of lives saved by one participant’s donation is not specified. A safer version would describe perceived concentration of impact, not confirmed lives saved.
issues.quote: For the case of an identifiable victim, given that the reference group is salient with the victim himself serving as the reference only, the proportion is as high as $100 \%$. While for the statistical victims, the reference group may consist of millions of people. Even though the absolute number of lives saved would be higher than a single individual, the proportion of lives saved would be reduced, thus evokes less helping behaviour.

issues.subcategory: Availability and affect mechanisms are blurred
issues.description: Availability and affect mechanisms are blurred: The mechanism in this paragraph is difficult to pin down. It introduces the availability heuristic as ease of retrieving instances from memory, but then explains the identifiable-victim effect mainly through affective reactions such as sympathy and distress, which are the specific affective variables measured later. If the intended account is availability leading to affect, or an affective mechanism rather than availability per se, that distinction matters for the later hypotheses about deliberation and feelings. If affect is the mechanism being tested, make that the main explanation. Alternatively, if availability is meant to be part of the mechanism, add a sentence explaining how memory accessibility is expected to produce the measured affect in this task.
issues.quote: Another reason to explain the identifiable victim effect is attributed to different psychological reasoning mechanisms in making judgments. The "availability heuristic" (Tversky \& Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual (Small \& Loewenstein, 2003). The information we receive about this person may elicit stronger affective reactions such as sympathy and distress such that people are more motivated to offer support to people in need. In contrast, given the number representing the statistical victims fails to induce any major affective response, less altruistic behaviour would be expected. As such, affective feelings do play a role in the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: Replication rationale becomes conceptually unclear
issues.description: Replication rationale becomes conceptually unclear: The rationale in this paragraph becomes conceptually unclear when it moves from psychic numbing and weak affective responses to numerical victims to the claim that “law enforcement” should motivate action against mass murder. The empirical importance of the effect is understandable, but the institutional or policy implication is not clearly connected to the replication rationale.
issues.quote: Scholar citations of the article and many important follow-up theoretical and empirical articles, such as Slovic (2007). Solvic (2007) argued for the drawbacks of the phenomenon to raise awareness on our indifference of numerous death in genocide. He introduced different psychological research to account for the failure to elicit affective feelings from numeric values which are important to explore alternative strategies to boost people's moral feelings towards statistical victims. Solvic (2007) urged the public not to rely on our unreliable emotional responses but law enforcement to motivate actions protecting those suffering from mass murder. The study to be replicated was also covered in the meta-analysis conducted by Lee and Feeley (2016) to deduce the weighted effect.

issues.subcategory: The meta-analysis sentence overstates what the small pooled effect shows
issues.description: The meta-analysis sentence overstates what the small pooled effect shows: The sentence moves from a very small pooled estimate to a broad claim about practical importance. The topic may well merit replication because the original article is influential and the effect has policy relevance, but an average effect size of 0.05 does not by itself support a claim about fundraising impact. Reframe the point: the article is worth revisiting because it is widely cited, while the broader literature suggests that the average effect may be small.
issues.quote: Although the overall mean effect size was only 0.05 , the significance of the identifiable victim effect is still crucial to encourage altruistic behaviour towards the needy, especially adopted widely in the fundraising campaign to promote charitable giving.

issues.subcategory: Study 3 effect size is not compatible with the bounded donation scale
issues.description: Study 3 effect size is not compatible with the bounded donation scale: The d = 0.23 benchmark is not compatible with the stated Study 3 contrast if that contrast is identifiable victim versus joint presentation. The means in Table 2 are 2.38 and 1.43, a difference of 0.95. On a 0–5 donation scale, a variable with mean μ has variance at most μ(5−μ); using μ = 2.38 and μ = 1.43 gives maximum SDs of about 2.50 and 2.26, and a maximum pooled SD around 2.38. The smallest possible standardized difference for a 0.95 mean gap is therefore about 0.40. A reported d of 0.23 would require a pooled SD above 4.1, which the bounded scale cannot produce. If 0.23 comes from a different comparison or from converting the omnibus F test, label it that way. Otherwise, recalculate the effect size and CI for the Study 3 implicit-debiasing contrast.
issues.quote: In Study 3, the effect of implicitly activating the analytical thinking mechanism on donation was $\mathrm{d}=0.23,95 \% \mathrm{Cl}[0.01,0.45]$, regarded as a small effect.

issues.subcategory: ANOVA statistics are placed on individual level rows
issues.description: ANOVA statistics are placed on individual level rows: Table 1 repeats the same F, p, and partial eta-squared values on the rows for the individual condition means. In an ANOVA, F = 6.75 tests the factor contrast across levels; it is not a separate inferential test of each level. Leave the inferential statistics on the factor row and show only M and SD for the identifiable and statistical rows. The same fix should be applied to the intervention rows if they follow the same pattern.
issues.quote:
Variations | M | SD | df1 | df2 | F | p | np2
Identifiability | | | 1 | 115 | 6.75 | <.05* | . 06
Identifiable victim | 2.12 | 2.13 | 1 | 115 | 6.75 | <. $05^{*}$ | . 06
Statistical victim | 1.21 | 1.67 | 1 | 115 | 6.75 | <. $05^{*}$ | . 06

issues.subcategory: Extension framed as mediation but analyzed as means
issues.description: Extension framed as mediation but analyzed as means: The perceived-impact extension is motivated with mediation language, but the stated hypothesis and planned analyses appear to test only condition differences in perceived impact. If perceived impact is intended as a mediator of donation, the analysis plan does not specify the donation link or an indirect-effect test; if it is only a parallel dependent variable, the mediation framing overstates what the extension can establish.
issues.quote: Yet, there were mixed findings regarding the mediation effect of perceived impact on the identifiable victim effect. Both Lee and Feeley(2016), and Friedrich and McGuire (2010) did not find support for the perceived impact, showing no difference in the helping behaviour between a personalized individual and anonymous groups of people. This highlights the importance of how the perceived impact of donation is linked with the identifiable victim effect in this replication. It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.

issues.subcategory: Confounding affective and cognitive measures in aggregated variable
issues.description: Confounding affective and cognitive measures in aggregated variable: There seems to be an issue with the “aggregated feelings” construct. The overview describes post-donation measures mainly as cognitive evaluations, while the hypotheses refer to affective feelings; Table 5 then appears to aggregate affective items with moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact. Because Hypothesis 5 concerns affective feelings and Hypothesis 6 treats perceived impact as a separate extension, combining these items into one aggregate would make the construct difficult to interpret. Perceived impact is an efficacy belief, not an affect item, and including it would change the dependent variable being compared with the original study. State the exact items in the aggregated-feelings score, exclude perceived impact from that score so it can be analyzed separately, and ensure the composite reflects only the intended affective measures.
issues.quote: After the donation, they had to fill up a questionnaire for different cognitive evaluations they experienced which may influence their choice of donation. These items included beliefs about the severity of the crisis, the perceived trustworthiness of the charity, the expected accountability of funds, evaluation of organizational efficiency, and the appropriateness of donation to help the victims.

issues.subcategory: Design/Procedures conflict on assignment structure
issues.description: Design/Procedures conflict on assignment structure: The Design and Procedures sections appear to give incompatible accounts of assignment. The design is called within-subject, the procedure says participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions, and the planned 2 × 3 ANOVA/cell structure elsewhere reads like a between-subjects factorial design. This between-subjects assumption is further evidenced in the Results section, where the six Table 7 cell counts sum to N = 1000, and Table 9's residual df = 994 equals N minus the six cells. This should be resolved because the assignment structure determines the causal interpretation and the appropriate error terms for the analyses, and the simulated pipeline is uninterpretable until the design/assignment description and planned ANOVA model are aligned.
issues.quote:
Design
We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively. The experimental design can be retrieved from the supplementary under the section of "Table of design".Table of design

## Procedures

Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions. The session of "Procedure" in the supplementary summarizes the procedure of the current replication study.

issues.subcategory: Mismatch in target effect size for replication evaluation
issues.description: Mismatch in target effect size for replication evaluation: The target effect size for evaluating the “effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect” appears to be mismatched. Earlier, $d=0.48$ is identified as the main effect of identifiability; the deliberative-thinking debiasing claim is more closely tied to the intervention effect, the identifiability-by-intervention interaction, or a focused debiasing contrast. The paper should clarify which original effect is the benchmark for replication evaluation.
issues.quote: We aim to study the effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect by comparing the replication effect with the original effect ( $\mathrm{d}=0.48,95 \% \mathrm{Cl}[0.11,0.84]$ ) obtained from the power analysis using the criteria set by Lebel, Vanpaemel, Cheung, and Campbell (2019) (see Figure 1).

issues.subcategory: Pairwise follow-ups should not depend on significant main effects
issues.description: Pairwise follow-ups should not depend on significant main effects: The gatekeeping rule is too restrictive for a factorial design. An interaction can appear even when neither main effect is significant. For example, in a 2×2 design with cell means 5, 0, 0, and 5, both marginal means are equal across each factor, but the interaction difference-in-differences is 10. The planned follow-ups should therefore be tied to the effect being interpreted: marginal pairwise comparisons after a main effect, and prespecified simple-effect or cell-contrast tests after an interaction.
issues.quote: | Bonferroni -adjusted pairwise comparisons (Note: We conduct the test only if the effect of identifiability and intervention are significant) | a. effect of identifiability on donation (with joint condition) | a.effect of identifiability on donation (with joint condition) b. effect of intervention on donation (with joint condition) c. interaction of identifiability and intervention on donation (with joint condition)

issues.subcategory: Correlation analysis does not define the unit of analysis
issues.description: Correlation analysis does not define the unit of analysis: The phrase “across six different conditions” leaves the unit of analysis open. A Pearson correlation could be computed over condition means, or over participant-level observations pooled within the listed conditions. Those are different estimands. Say explicitly that the planned analysis is a participant-level Pearson correlation between the aggregated-feelings score and donation, computed within each condition or pooled across specified conditions. If pooling is used, report whether condition indicators are controlled.
issues.quote: Correlation between aggregated feelings and donation | Linear Pearson's correlation | correlation between aggregated feelings and donation across four different conditions (statistical/intervention, statistical/no intervention, identifiable/intervention, identifiable/no intervention) | correlation between aggregated feelings and donation across six different conditions (statistical/intervention, statistical/no intervention, identifiable/intervention, identifiable/no intervention, joint/intervention, joint/no intervention)

issues.subcategory: Replication classification seems unsupported by deviations
issues.description: Replication classification seems unsupported by deviations: The “close to very close replication” label seems stronger than Table 6 alone supports. The table lists several departures that may matter for interpreting replication success, especially hypothetical rather than consequential donations, the online MTurk setting and participant context, intervention applied to the joint condition, and changed feeling measures. The classification may still be defensible, but the basis for treating these deviations as compatible with “close to very close” should be made clearer.
issues.quote:
Table 6
Classification of the replication, based on Lebel et al. (2018)
[TABLE]
Design facet | Replication | Details of deviation
IV operationalization | Same | /
DV operationalization | Similar | /
IV stimuli | Similar | Updated victim information We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.
Intervention applied to the joint condition To combine study 1 and 3 into a single study, intervention will be applied to the joint condition to allow the comparison of explicit and implicit manipulation with fewer confounds.
DV stimuli | Different | Question adjustment We made minor changes to the questions evaluating participants' feelings to specify the emotion they experienced to the victim information they have just read Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from \$0 to \$5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc effect-size column is not Cohen’s d in Tables 10 and 14
issues.description: Post-hoc effect-size column is not Cohen’s d in Tables 10 and 14: The numbers under “d” in Tables 10 and 14 match a correlation-style effect size, not Cohen’s d. For the first row of Table 10, sqrt(t²/(t²+df)) = sqrt(2.40²/(2.40²+994)) = .076, exactly the value in the table. A standardized mean difference would be about |t|sqrt(1/334 + 1/334) = .19 using the marginal identifiable and statistical sample sizes from Table 7, with the sign depending on contrast coding. Additionally, the corresponding CI crosses zero despite a Bonferroni-significant pairwise p value. Relabel the column as r and give r intervals, or compute Cohen’s d and its confidence interval on the same scale used for the original-effect comparisons.

issues.subcategory: Narrative reverses the identifiable and statistical donation means
issues.description: Narrative reverses the identifiable and statistical donation means: The interpretation swaps the condition means. Table 7 gives an identifiable-victim marginal mean of (2.58×159 + 2.50×175)/334 = 2.54, and a statistical-victim marginal mean of (2.46×175 + 2.01×159)/334 = 2.25. The combined SDs are about 1.76 and 1.67, respectively. The text should say that giving was higher in the identifiable condition than in the statistical condition, unless the table labels are reversed. Also align the sign of t with the chosen contrast direction; the current negative t is hard to read next to the stated group ordering.
issues.quote: From Table 10, we noticed that there is a significant difference between identifiable and statistical victim condition, $\mathrm{t}(994)=-2.40$, $\mathrm{SE}=0.13, \mathrm{p}=.049$, meaning that participants who faced a statistical victim ( $\mathrm{M}=2.54, \mathrm{SD}=1.76$ ) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims ( $\mathrm{M}=2.24$, $\mathrm{SD}=1.67$ ).

issues.subcategory: The one-cell-versus-five-cells contrast does not explain the interaction
issues.description: The one-cell-versus-five-cells contrast does not explain the interaction: This contrast may be a planned comparison, but it does not unpack the 2×3 interaction. From Table 7, the intervention differences are identifiable: 2.58−2.50 = 0.08; statistical: 2.46−2.01 = 0.45; joint: 2.37−2.67 = −0.30. The interaction concerns those changing differences. Averaging five cells together hides that pattern and answers a different question. Report simple effects or planned interaction contrasts, and present the one-versus-five comparison only as a separate contrast if it was preregistered for that purpose.
issues.quote: Given the significant interaction effect, we also conducted a t -test to study if the mean of identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation. This replication did not find any difference between the donation under the identifiable/no intervention condition and combination of other conditions, $\mathrm{t}(998)=0.59, \mathrm{p}=.558$, contrary to the significant result found in the original study.

{"overall": "**Placeholder narratives and empirical claims**

The manuscript notes that the current version is built on simulated Qualtrics data. Readers will notice that empirical claims remain integrated throughout the abstract, Method, Results, and open-science sections, including definitive statements such as "found no empirical support," "Results have supported the hypothesis," and "data collection was completed before analyses."

To function as a final empirical report, the document requires a transition away from the template format to report actual recruitment sources, final exclusions, descriptive statistics, and inferential tests based exclusively on the final dataset. Reconciling the text to reflect the actual data collection phase will prevent confusion regarding the evidential standing of the findings across the manuscript.

**Procedural descriptions of the experimental design**

The basic experimental design structure presents conflicting descriptions across different sections. The Design section specifies "a single within-subject design," the Results tables present a $2 \times 3$ matrix consistent with a between-subjects structure, and the Procedure states that "participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions."

Because the source material relied on randomized experiments, the inferential weight of the replication requires condition comparability. Clarifying whether the design relies on random assignment, establishing the exact condition allocation procedure, and explicitly confirming if participants viewed more than one victim condition will ensure the structural logic aligns with the core replication objectives.

**Hypothetical versus physical donation behaviour**

Table 6 indicates that the replication employs an "imaginary donation" from $\$0$ to $\$5$, departing from Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic's Study 1, which endowed participants with physical money and measured actual giving. The paper currently classifies this study as a "close to very close" replication.

Because the target identifiable victim effect manifests as a tangible relinquishing of resources, the shift to hypothetical donation alters baseline giving levels, response variance, and the psychological meaning of the dependent variable. The manuscript requires a rationale detailing how this adaptation operates psychologically and how the shift from physical to hypothetical resources informs the exact classification and boundary conditions of the replication claims.

**Combination of the target studies**

The paper combines the original studies into a joint methodological framework. Small et al. (2007) tested explicit instruction in Study 1 using a $2 \times 2$ grid, and tested implicit comparative exposure in Study 3 using a three-condition structure absent explicit instruction. Integrating these tests into a merged $2 \times 3$ design creates a novel experimental cell combining explicit debiasing instruction with implicit exposure to victim statistics.

Table 3 does not outline a specific hypothesis for this combined explicit-plus-joint condition, and the contrast matrices in Table 5 group original replication conditions together with these newly created extension cells. Separating the primary, direct comparative tests mapped to Study 1 and Study 3 from exploratory tests on the novel combinations will clarify exactly which cells constitute the formal replication set.

**Statistical framing for replication evaluation**

The statistical framework relies predominantly on omnibus $2 \times 3$ ANOVAs, post-hoc decomposition, and partial eta-squared metrics, whereas the guiding Lebel et al. framework evaluates replications using planned, comparable effects. The central replication hypotheses are fundamentally anchored to specific contrasts, such as the interaction originally observed in Study 1 and the identifiable-versus-joint comparison derived from Study 3.

The power planning sections appropriately utilize the Study 1 identifiability effect ($d = 0.48$) but do not articulate power models for the smaller Study 3 effect, the critical interaction term, or the perceived-impact extension. Incorporating comparable standardized effects with confidence intervals for each targeted planned contrast will align the reported tests cleanly with modern replication-evaluation standards.

**Operationalization of the perceived-impact extension**

The introduction connects perceived impact to proportion dominance and perceived efficacy, yet the analytic plan shifts between treating it as a segregated feeling item, part of an affective battery, and a standalone extension. Hypothesis 6 predicts only that identifiable victims elicit higher perceived impact, while the central deliberative debiasing manipulation is not linked theoretically to perceived impact at all.

Detailing whether perceived impact is positioned theoretically as an outcome, a mediator, or a moderator will elevate this item mechanically.
